sections.heading: Mixer calibration problem
sections.body: A small mixer applies H(s) = 2(1 + s/800)/(1 + s/3200). The service log stores angular frequency in radians per second. A colleague wrote the two break values directly on a hertz axis. Draw a corrected axis and label each break using f = omega/(2 pi). Give the limiting low- and high-frequency gains as both ratios and decibels.

sections.heading: Check one point numerically
sections.body: Evaluate |H(j omega)| at omega = 1600 rad/s, retaining the squared magnitude until the final square root. Compare the result with the straight-line Bode approximation in that region. Explain why 20 log10 is the appropriate conversion for this gain.

sections.heading: Record the checks
sections.body: Show the algebra and label the numerical axes with units. Report one independent check outside the transition band, picking a frequency at least one decade from a break. A correct limiting slope alone does not identify the two break frequencies.

sections.heading: An instrument discrepancy
sections.body: The display reports 9.1 dB at the test point. Your answer need not match that unverified reading exactly. Check whether the instrument divides by the input peak, RMS value or full scale. Write down which convention your calculation assumes and give a plausible sign for the error caused by applying a peak/RMS correction twice. Attach the two gain limits, the intermediate complex magnitude and the final labeled plot.

pdf.title: Triangular wave reconstruction at the monitor output

sections.heading: Source waveform
sections.body: A line tester generates an even triangular signal with period T and amplitude A. On the interval -T/2 through T/2, write it as x(t) = A - 4A|t|/T, then continue periodically. The printed monitor trace has a positive peak at t = 0 and a negative peak at t = T/2. Use omega0 = 2 pi/T and the cosine-series convention x(t) = a0/2 + sum a_n cos(n omega0 t).

sections.heading: 1. Sketch and separate the terms
sections.body: Sketch two periods with a common baseline. On your sketch, show a half-period shift and use it to say which harmonic indices can contribute. Explain why the sine coefficients vanish under the specified time origin. If you choose another origin, draw the shift before writing coefficients.

sections.heading: 2. Work the coefficients
sections.body: Set up the cosine integral over half a period and show the boundary terms after integration by parts. Evaluate the first three nonzero a_n in terms of A and pi. Keep each sign in your written table and label the frequency of each term in hertz for a 100 Hz fundamental.

sections.heading: 3. Check the partial reconstruction
sections.body: Use A = 1 V and T = 0.01 s for an independent numerical check. Evaluate the three-term sum at t = 0, t = T/4 and t = T/2; compare with the piecewise source values. State one reason a truncated series can miss the magnitude of a peak while still giving the correct sign. A calculator or a short local script is enough.

sections.heading: Check a time-shift claim
sections.body: A note on the bench claims that shifting the capture origin by T/4 keeps all sine terms equal to zero. Test this with the fundamental, using cos(a+b). Identify which coefficient changes and explain why the physical signal still has the same period. Include a corrected sketch of the axes and one line of algebra.

sections.heading: Return a short work packet
sections.body: Hand in the labeled sketch, your integral with boundary terms, the coefficient table, and the numerical check. Mark units on each numerical line. If an evaluation differs from the original waveform, indicate whether the discrepancy is due to finite truncation, a normalization choice or a possible arithmetic error. No recording or online demonstration is required.

sections.heading: Compare two hand sketches
sections.body: An older notebook gives a nonzero even term and places the positive peak at T/4. Look at the time origin, offset and symmetry separately. Which discrepancy could be explained by a horizontal shift alone? Which would require a different source waveform or an incorrect integral? Use a concrete sample from your table to defend each answer. Do not erase the original sketch; circle the feature that distinguishes the two versions.
